I.       INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE.

         This proceeding involves the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC

and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation to amend their Certificates of Convenience and

Necessity for the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line

Project—a proposed high-voltage transmission line spanning approximately 223 miles across

fifteen Texas counties. 1 This Initial Brief will focus on issues relating to the Route (Preliminary

Order No. 8) that best meets the regulatory and statutory criteria. BCI acknowledges there are

legitimate concerns that have been raised by several parties relating to the need for Import Path 2.

BCI did not submit direct evidence on these issues, and so does not attempt to evaluate the evidence

relating to them here. BCI reserves the right to reply to arguments on the need issues (Preliminary

Order Issues 5, 6, and 7) in its Reply Brief.

         The ALJs and Commission must now determine which of the filed routes best meets the

statutory and regulatory criteria governing route selection under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and

PUC Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B). Compelling evidence establishes that Route 392 is that

route.

Applicants acknowledged at the hearing that their route analysis, including the selection of Route

field-level investigation of actual conditions along the proposed corridors. Applicants’ witness

surveys or borings, and would not presume to know more about a landowner’s tract than the

landowner. 2

neither reflects the qualitative factors the statute requires the Commission to weigh, including

community values, environmental integrity, and the characteristics of the land the proposed routes

would cross. That information was supplied at the hearing by landowners and independent experts

with firsthand knowledge of conditions along both corridors—information unavailable to either

Applicants or Staff at the time their recommendations were developed.

II.        THE PROJECT SHOULD CROSS THE COLORADO RIVER IN THE LEAST

is not in dispute. The threshold policy-level question the ALJs and Commission must answer is

where that crossing should occur. As Andrew H. Sansom, Ph.D., who served for twelve years as

Executive Director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department and brings decades of professional

experience in conservation, water resources, and public land stewardship in Texas, testified: “From

a conservation perspective, the primary question is where that crossing can occur in a manner that

does the least harm to the character of the river and to the surrounding environment.” 5

         The Colorado River crossing decision is the clearest policy choice presented in this

proceeding. The Commission’s route selection analysis under Texas Utilities Code

§ 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) is not a property-level or county-level exercise. The statutory factors—

environmental integrity, community values, recreational and park areas, aesthetic values, and

compatible rights-of-way—operate at the scale of the study area as a whole, and they require the

Commission to identify and weigh the factors that distinguish one route from another.

        No factor distinguishes the available routes more clearly than the choice of where to cross

the Colorado River. That choice carries consequences extending well beyond the boundaries of

any single property or county and implicates natural resources of statewide significance. The

record on this point includes the testimony of former Public Utility Commission Chairman Barry

Smitherman and former Texas Parks and Wildlife Department Executive Director Andrew H.

Sansom, Ph.D., two witnesses whose professional experience and public service have given them

a statewide view of the resources at stake. 18 Both testified that the Colorado River and the State

Parks along it represent the most significant environmental and conservation consideration in this

study area—not only for the communities and landowners situated within that area, and not only

for ERCOT ratepayers, but for the State of Texas as a whole. 19

abandoned links to the northern alternative route network. 23 Link J6 was also shortened by one-

        B. The Marginal Cost Advantage Attributed to Route 894 Is Unreliable and Does Not
           Support Route Selection.

        The Applicants’ estimated cost for Route 894 is $1,680,919,000. The estimated cost for

Route 392 is $1,715,218,000. The difference is $34,299,000, or approximately 2.04 percent. 39

While thirty-four million dollars is not a trivial sum, in the context of a project whose estimated

transmission line costs range from approximately $1.64 billion to $1.86 billion, the difference is

marginal. Furthermore, PUC Staff witness John Poole, P.E., confirmed in deposition that the cost

spread across the filed routes in this proceeding is tight relative to comparable projects—spanning

only 10 percent from the least expensive route to the most expensive. 40

        The cost difference falls within another band as well. Applicants’ engineering witness

Corin Cooley testified that the cost contingency for this project is between 10 and 15 percent. 41 A

contingency range of 10 to 15 percent on a project of this scale represents an uncertainty of $168

million to $257 million in either direction. The cost estimates are, by the Applicants’ own

characterization, projections based on assumptions about structure counts, labor rates, and

construction conditions that will not be known with precision until detailed engineering is

complete. Given those understandable uncertainties for a project of this scale, placing significant
